Weekly "Merge main branch into dev-1.37" sync PRs against `kubernetes/website` fail the **EasyCLA** check with `Missing CLA Authorization`, and the only committer flagged is the bot identity `kubernetes-prow[bot]`.

title: StatefulSet pod revisions not updated when MaxUnavailableStatefulSet enabled
description:
### What happened?

I decided to open this issue after investigating https://github.com/stackabletech/trino-operator/issues/854.

The high level description of the problem is that the stateful set controller doesn't update the pods according to the latest STS revision and the pods are left crashlooping **if the first revision is faulty** and can never become available. This doesn't happen if the `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature is disabled.

Unfortunately I cannot create a much simpler example, but I attach the relevant controller log messages below.

Based on these logs you can see that:

1. The Stackable Operator for Trino (`trino-op` from now on) creates two `StatefulSet` objects with a single replica. They both expose the same problem, so for simplicity, I will use only one of them from now on (`trino-coordinator-default`).
2. The initial revision of this sts is `trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8`. This first STS  revision has a faulty command args  and can never become available.
3. The `trino-op` updates the sts rapidly to the revision `trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59`. Now the STS command args are correct and the pods should be able to become ready.
4. The pod created initially is never updated so it never becomes ready.

To summarize my understanding, the sts revision is never updated if the pod never becomes ready, and the pod doesn't become ready because it has an old revision.

description:
### What happened?

With `WorkloadWithJob` enabled, a Job whose name is 58+ characters never starts pods. The Job controller names the PodGroupTemplate `<job-name>-pgt-0` ([job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/pkg/controller/job/job_scheduling_manager.go#L518-L521)), and `spec.podGroupTemplates[].name` is a DNS label limited to 63 bytes ([types.go#L218](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0887d3330e9bb0489dac763160f2ca27702e7729/staging/src/k8s.io/api/scheduling/v1beta1/types.go#L218)). description:
### What happened?

`PSIData.Total` in the kubelet Summary API is documented as nanoseconds, and KEP-4205 says the same. With the default cadvisor stats provider the kubelet reports the cgroup's raw value, which is in microseconds. With `PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI` enabled the value comes from containerd in nanoseconds. So the same field differs by 1000x depending on how the node collects stats.

Same pod on two nodes of a v1.37.0 cluster, one using cadvisor stats and one using CRI stats, compared against the container's own `cpu.pressure`:

| node | stats | Summary `cpu.psi.some.total` | cgroup `cpu.pressure` some total (us) |
|---|---|---|---|

| worker | CRI | 74156229000 | 74196804 |

The cadvisor value lags because the Summary is cached, but it is clearly microseconds. The CRI value is 1000x the cgroup counter.

### What did you expect to happen?

`total` in nanoseconds on both paths, as documented.

A kind cluster with two v1.37.0 nodes, the worker started with `--feature-gates=PodAndContainerStatsFromCRI=true`. Run a CPU-limited busy pod on each node, then compare:

description:
### What happened?

With `memoryReservationPolicy: TieredReservation`, an in-place resize that changes only the memory request updates the container's `memory.low` but leaves the pod cgroup's `memory.low` at the old request. It doesn't recover on later syncs.

Measured on v1.37.0 (kind, containerd, cgroup v2), Burstable pod, limit 512Mi:

|---|---|---|---|

| request-only resize to 400Mi | 419430400 | **268435456** | 536870912 |

description:
### What happened?

With MemoryQoS on and a `memoryThrottlingFactor` set, I resized a Burstable container's memory request up to its limit in place. The container kept the `memory.high` computed for its previous request, so it stays throttled below its limit. It doesn't recover on later syncs.

| 400Mi (resize) | 525123584 (recomputed, correct) |

description:
### What happened?

With `ResourceHealthStatus` enabled, kubelet can change the order of entries in `status.containerStatuses[*].allocatedResourcesStatus` even when device and claim health have not changed.

There are two nondeterministic paths in kubelet v1.36.3:

Kubelet should produce a stable `AllocatedResourcesStatus` representation when resource health is unchanged. Both the outer `[]ResourceStatus` and each inner `[]ResourceHealth` should have deterministic ordering, so repeated syncs do not cause unnecessary Pod status updates.

If the subordinate ID pool kubelet uses for user namespaces changes between restarts, and a pod on disk holds a mapping that falls outside the new pool, the kubelet does not start:

title: cgroup v2: CPU weights saturate for Pod containers requesting 256 or more CPUs
description:
### What happened?

On cgroup-v2 nodes, CPU weights stop increasing once a container's CPU request reaches 256 CPUs. Larger requests therefore receive the same relative CPU scheduling weight.

Kubelet converts CPU requests to shares using 1024 shares per CPU, capped at `262144`. Both 256-CPU and 288-CPU requests consequently produce `262144` shares. See [`MilliCPUToShares()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go).

Kubelet's Pod-cgroup conversion also maps shares at or above `262144` to `cpu.weight=10000`. See [`getCPUWeight()`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/cgroup_manager_linux.go).

We observed this ceiling at both the Pod and application-container levels on a 384-logical-CPU node. In an experiment with kubelet's `MaxShares` raised to `294912` (1024 x 288), the results were:

| CPU request | Container OCI shares | Pod `cpu.weight` | Container `cpu.weight` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 256 | 262144 | 10000 | 10000 |

### What happened?

An informer can deliver a delete of a PodGroup (PG) / CompositePodGroup (CPG) followed by a create of an object with the same namespace/name as a single `UpdateFunc(old, new)` call. This happens whenever both operations fall into a watch gap and the reflector relists (`DeltaFIFO.Replace`): the handler sees an update whose old and new have different UIDs, and the scheduler never observes the intermediate deletion. title: e2e_node: make ImageGCPeriod (and other e2e_node wait budgets) configurable for tests
description:
## What happened
While removing duplicated `[Slow]` spec execution between `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-serial` and `ci-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd-slow` (kubernetes/test-infra#37903), we looked into why the `[Slow]`-tagged ImageGC/GarbageCollect/MirrorPod specs in `test/e2e_node` cost ~30 minutes per host.

It's not image size or pull time — these use the standard few-MB e2e-test-images (pause, busybox, nginx-slim/agnhost). The time comes from wait/poll budgets hardcoded in the tests themselves, bound to production defaults:

- `image_gc_test.go`: two `[Slow]` specs poll for up to `checkGCUntil = 6 * time.Minute`, gated by kubelet's `ImageGCPeriod` (hardcoded to 5 minutes).
- `garbage_collector_test.go`: `setupDuration = 10 * time.Minute`, `garbageCollectDuration = 3 * time.Minute`.
- `mirror_pod_test.go`: several `2 * time.Minute` `Eventually` polls, plus a couple `5 * time.Minute` waits.

Polling more frequently doesn't help — these tests aren't slow because they check infrequently, they're waiting on a real kubelet-side event gated by a fixed period.

## What we'd like
Make `ImageGCPeriod` (and whatever governs the GC/mirror-pod wait windows above) configurable for e2e_node tests, so these specs aren't bound to the 5-minute production default and can run with a much shorter period in test.

## Context
- kubernetes/test-infra#37903 (merged) — removed duplicate execution of these specs as a stopgap

Two additive, opt-in changes to the CRI container/pod list calls so the kubelet's PLEG can stop decoding data it doesn't use:

description:
### What happened?

On current Kubernetes master, the DRA kubelet plugin helper can generate an unusable automatic service socket endpoint when rolling updates are enabled with a valid long driver name.

With normal defaults:

```text
plugin directory:
/var/lib/kubelet/plugins/<driver name>

rolling service socket:
dra-<Pod UID>.sock
```

With a normal 36-byte Pod UID:

```text

Linux 6.7 added support for ["remote partitions"](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#:~:text=partition%20is%20created.-,cpuset.cpus.partition,-A%20read%2Dwrite), which enables containers to allocate exclusive CPUs without modifying any other cgroups. Currently, with static CPU policy, cpu_manager runs a reconcile loop (default 10s period) to sync CPU allocation to containers. The default set is updated (for every container) to remove CPUs as they're allocated exclusively.

3. Every static CPU assignment (or release) requires updating every other container on the node. These are all done through `UpdateContainerResources` requests, and are subject to global NRI locks.

description:
### What happened?

With the static Memory Manager, pod-scope Topology Manager, and `PodLevelResourceManagers` enabled, pod-level allocation is persisted through independent checkpoint updates: `PodMemoryAssignments` first, then per-container assignments, then `MachineState`. On restart, `validateState` reconstructs expected accounting by iterating `ContainerMemoryAssignments`. description:
### What happened?

Stopping a probe worker does not cancel a probe that is already executing. `worker.stop()` does a non-blocking send on `stopCh`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L204-L211

and `run()` only selects on `stopCh` between probes, after `doProbe` returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L186-L201

So when `RemovePod` / `CleanupPods` / `StopLivenessAndStartup` stops a worker, an exec probe that is mid-flight keeps running against a container that is being killed. It ends only when its own `TimeoutSeconds` elapses, and `runProbeWithRetries` will retry up to `maxProbeRetries` (3) if the attempt errors, so the worst case is roughly `3 * TimeoutSeconds` after `stop()`. `TimeoutSeconds` is user-controlled, so that can be minutes. The worker also records the result of that last probe after it was told to stop.

Between #130487 (v1.35.0) and #140882 this happened to be papered over: workers inherited the pod worker's sync context, which the pod worker cancels at teardown, so in-flight execs died promptly. That was not a fix, it was the cause of #140881. The same cancellation also killed every readiness probe for the entire grace period, which is the much worse bug. #140882 detaches the worker context with `context.WithoutCancel` and restores the pre-1.35 behavior, which reinstates this gap.

title: Memory Manager pod scope drops hugepage requests used only by regular init containers
description:
### What happened?

With the static Memory Manager and pod-level Topology Manager scope, `getPodRequestedResources` drops a memory resource type when that resource is requested by a regular init container but by no app container.
﻿
A minimal example is:
﻿
- a regular init container requests `memory: 1Gi` and `hugepages-1Gi: 2Gi`;
- the app container requests `memory: 1Gi`, but does not request `hugepages-1Gi`.
﻿
The calculated pod request is:
﻿
```text
map[memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The expected result is:
﻿
```text
map[hugepages-1Gi:2147483648 memory:1073741824]
```
﻿
The init container still receives an individual hugepage memory block because its resources are processed separately, but the pod allocation and global NUMA capacity do not account for that block. This can produce incorrect topology hints and leave the Memory Manager machine state with more available hugepage capacity than actually assigned.

### What did you expect to happen?

getPodRequestedResources` should calculate each managed resource independently across the union of resource names requested by:
﻿
- app containers;
- restartable init containers;
- regular init containers.
﻿
For every resource name, the existing init-container and long-running-container maximum semantics should then be applied. A resource must not be omitted merely because no app container requests that resource type.
